sentences.text: This dinosaur possessed a large head measuring 1.8 meters from snout to frill tip, featuring a prominent nasal horn but lacking forehead horns. Its neck frill was short and rounded with smooth edges and moderately large openings.
The animal had a robust body with longer hind legs than front legs and a tail held elevated off the ground.
Contrary to popular belief, the name does not mean single horn but rather single sprout, describing how its teeth grew compared to a relative named double sprout.
A bone originally thought to be a squamosal in one specimen was actually identified as a pterygoid.
The type and only specimen of Monoclonius lowei was recovered from the upper strata of the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta.
Edward Drinker Cope first named the genus Monoclonius in 1876, establishing the type species Monoclonius crassus during that same year.
Lawrence Lambe later described three new species of Monoclonius from Canada in 1902 based on fragmentary skulls.
As a herbivore, it likely fed on dominant plants of its time, such as ferns and conifers.
It used a beak made of keratin to cut food, which it then chewed with a battery of teeth in the back, keeping food in its mouth with cheek-like organs.

Monoclonius is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Sauropsida, superorder Dinosauria, order Ornithischia, suborder Neornithischia, infraorder Ceratopsia, family Ceratopsidae, and subfamily Centrosaurinae.

Many specimens previously classified as Monoclonius are now believed to be juvenile or subadult Centrosaurus or other genera, leading to the view that the name is often considered a nomen dubium pending further study.
The animal lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically within the Campanian stage from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

It is debated whether the original type material of Monoclonius crassus belongs to a centrosaurine or a hadrosaurian, with some evidence suggesting it might be a hadrosaurian mistakenly associated with other fossils.

In 1997, Scott Sampson and colleagues concluded that Monoclonius crassus and comparable specimens were nomina dubia because they represented juveniles or subadults, evidenced by their juvenile long-grained bone structure. In 1998, Peter Dodson and Allison Tumarkin argued that the bone structure of Monoclonius specimens could be explained by species-specific pedomorphosis, where adults retain juvenile traits.

The developing consensus suggests that the genus Monoclonius is constrained to the type species M. crassus, specifically the lectotype frill from the Judith River Formation of Montana. Some paleontologists believe that fossils identified as Monoclonius were possibly Centrosaurus of different ages or sexes, making the existence of the genus unclear. During the 1990s, the relationship between Monoclonius and Centrosaurus remained a subject of debate.
